2. The relevant facts, for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioners as pre-emptors instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 102 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Lakshmipur for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act alleging that the land as described in the Schedule of the application for pre-emption belonged to Manzuma Khatun, the vendor-opposite party No. 2 who transferred the said land by a deed executed on 16-4-1998 to the pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 Abu Hanif Howlader. The said deed was presented for registration on 24-4-1998 and ultimately the same was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 10-3-1999. The said deed was executed and registered in the form of a deed of exchange. The pre-emptors knew the said deed as deed of exchange. But the vendor Manzuma Khatun went to the house of her father in the middle of September 2000 and at the time of talking the pre-emptor No. 1 asked her as to whether she had constructed any structure in the land at Mohammadpur, Dhaka, which she got in lieu of exchange, or not. Then she replied that she did not exchange the disputed land and she had sold the same. The said deed was executed and registered in the form of deed of exchange, only to avoid pre-emption. After execution of the deed of exchange she had returned the land. The pre-emptor knowing about it, at first, collected the certified copy of the deed of exchange. Thereafter on 19-10-2000 he collected the certified copy of deed of retransfer as executed by the vendor Manzuma to the pre-emptee in respect of the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza, under Police Station Mohammadpur, Dhaka and confirmed that the instant transaction was, in fact, out and out a sale, but the pre-emptee and the vendor, in collusion with each other, made the same in the form of deed of exchange only to avoid pre-emption. Thereafter, the pre-emptors instituted the instant application for pre-emption on 30-11-2000. The pre-emptors also collected the certified copy of another Kabala deed in respect of the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza, where from it is detected that the pre-emptee, after taking return of the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza from the vendor Manjuma Khatun, had transferred the said land to one Anwara Khatun by executing Kabala deed dated 13-11-1999. In such view of the matter, the pre-emptors are entitled to get the disputed land by way of pre-emption. 

 3. The pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 contested the application for pre-emption by filing written objection denying all the material allegations contending that the instant application for pre-emption was not maintainable and the same was barred by section 96(10)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. His specific case, in short, was that he exchanged his land measuring 0.04 acre of Ramchandrapur Mouza under Police Station Mohammadpur, Dhaka in lieu of the disputed land. After so exchange, possession was delivered accordingly. The market price of the disputed land is more than Taka 16,00,000 (Taka Sixteen lacs). Earlier, admitting the deed of exchange the pre-emptors executed a Nadabipatra in favour of the pre-emptee when it was detected that some portion of the disputed land had been erroneously recorded in the names of the pre-emptors. After admitting the impugned deed as deed of exchange the pre-emptors cannot say that the same was a sale deed. It has further been staled that the pre-emptor had knowledge about the instant deed from the time of its execution. Subsequent story regarding the date of knowledge as mentioned by the pre-emptors is false. The instant application is barred by limitation. It has further been stated that the vendor Manzuma never executed and registered the sale deed dated 19-4-1998 in favour of the pre-emptee and the pre-emptee had not executed and registered any deed in favour of Anwara Khatun. In such view of the matter, the instant application for pre-emption was not maintainable so the same should be dismissed. 

 6. Mr. Quamrul Haque Siddiqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, while assailing the submission of Mr. Maswood, submits that Ext. 4(ka), is secondary evidence and the same has not been admitted in evidence on due compliance of sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act. He further submits that from plain reading of Ext.4 it appears that the same is a deed of exchange. So, the instant application for pre-emption is barred under section 96(10)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He further submits that sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act will operate as a bar to admit any oral evidence to contradict the contents of the register instruments. He further submits that as the pre-emptors failed to prove Ext’s. 4(ka) and 5 in accordance with law and there is no other direct or circumstantial evidence to prove that the instant transaction was out and out a sale and allegation of fraud as made by Mr. Maswood has not been established so the Courts below rightly disbelieved the story of fraud and the finding of the Courts below regarding fraud is finding of fact which cannot be interfered with by exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure by this Court. 

 "A registered document carries presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein and that one who disputes the said presumption is under the law required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement in the registered document. Exhibit 1 has been registered by the Munsif-Cum-Magistrate of Udaypur, Tripura State, India. Since defendant No.5 was disputing the genuineness of the registered document Exhibitl it was his duty to establish that there was nothing like Munsif; Magistrate, Official or Office in Udaypur in the Tripura State who was authorised to register irrevocable power of attorney. But the said defendant totally failed to bring on record any material where form it can be said Munsif/ Magistrate, Udaypur, Tripura State, India was not competent to register Exhibit 1. The fact is that exhibit 1 was revalidated and re-stamped by the Office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla. Official act has the presumption of correctness and that one who challenges or disputes that presumption of correctness is required to establish that by legal evidence." 

 13. In the case of Tambia Khatun vs Rafiquullah, reported in 2 ADC 838 it appears that in similar circumstances the High Court Division observed that "Section 92 will operate as a bar in respect of admissibility of oral evidence." In that case a certified copy of deed of retransfer was produced. The impugned deed was a deed of exchange, pre-emptor producing the certified copy of the deed of retransfer claimed that the instant transaction was colourable one and made only to avoid pre-emption. The High Court Division accepting the argument as advanced on behalf of the pre-emptee that the oral evidence contradicting the contents of the registered document will not be admissible in evidence as the impugned deed was a deed of exchange. So the application for pre-emption will also be barred under section 96(1)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thereafter Appeal was preferred and their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed: 

 14. Section 96 (10) (b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 reads as follows: 

 (a) transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase; or 

 16. Section 92 of the Evidence Act provides that when a document described in section 91 has been proved according to section 91, "no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted, as between the parties to any such instrument or their representatives in interest, for the purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to, or subtracting from, its terms.
